summary: Describes a protocol for running OSI Connectionless transport service on top of UDP. It was on the standards track and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1240 describes how to run the OSI connectionless transport service on top of UDP, the Internet's simple message protocol. Each transport message is built into a small header called a UD TPDU and sent as one ordinary UDP datagram. The aim was to let OSI applications work over the Internet while keeping the existing TCP and IP network in place.

subtitle: Running the OSI connectionless transport service on top of UDP, so OSI applications can use the Internet.

tldr.problem: The ISO and CCITT had defined well-built connectionless session, presentation and application services that TCP and UDP did not offer, and the Internet community wanted to run those OSI services over the Internet without disrupting what already worked.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a transport service access point whose services match the ISO 8072 connectionless transport service, and implements it by building a UD TPDU and sending it as a single UDP datagram. The two UDP service primitives, send datagram and read datagram, stand in for the connectionless network service primitives N-UNIT-DATA.REQUEST and N-UNIT-DATA.INDICATION.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1240 is Historic and the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. The memo expected that once OSI lower layers were widely implemented in the Internet, the UDP and IP services underneath would simply be replaced by them.

today: RFC 1240 is Historic, which means the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It has not been obsoleted by a later RFC, so no replacement is named. The memo's own plan was that, once OSI lower layers were widely implemented in the Internet, the UDP and IP services underneath would simply be replaced by them.

sections.title: Why the OSI Upper Layers over UDP
sections.content:
The Internet had a mature, well-developed set of layered transport and network protocols, offering both connection-oriented service through TCP and connectionless service through UDP over the connectionless network service of IP. Many popular applications had been built directly on top of them over the past decade, and they had helped the Internet protocols and services become widely spread de facto standards.

In the years before, the ISO and CCITT had defined a well-architected set of upper layer standards covering connection-oriented and connectionless session, presentation and application services and protocols. These offer services to application developers that the TCP and IP standards do not provide, such as dialogue control, transfer syntax, peer authentication and directory services. As RFC 1006 had already indicated, it is desirable to offer the OSI upper layer services directly in the Internet without disrupting existing facilities, which permits a more graceful convergence and transition strategy from IP-based networks to OSI-based networks.

The primary motivation for this memo is to gain experience with the OSI connectionless upper layer protocols: the connectionless session protocol S-UNIT-DATA, the connectionless presentation protocol P-UNIT-DATA, the connectionless ACSE protocol A-UNIT-DATA and the connectionless transport protocol T-UNIT-DATA. Although many OSI standard applications such as X.400 and FTAM are connection-oriented, the connectionless mode is appropriate for certain application classes. ISO SC21/WG6 identified request-response applications, broadcast and multicast, inward data collection, and migratory or unreliable processes, and the request-response client-server class is the most prominent. The memo argues that connection setup and tear-down exchanges and the complex connection-oriented protocol machines become unnecessary overhead for a simple request-response exchange, especially in reliable environments such as a LAN or ISDN.

The memo's conclusion is that offering an OSI connectionless transport service on top of the Internet allows future applications to use the OSI connectionless upper layer services that are required to conform to the OSI upper layer architecture. At the time, T-UNIT-DATA, S-UNIT-DATA, P-UNIT-DATA and A-UNIT-DATA had reached International Standard, and as such applications become widely available and OSI lower layer service is widely implemented in the Internet, the underlying UDP and IP services can simply be replaced with the OSI lower layers.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISO and CCITT had written good standards for the upper layers of a network, including services that TCP and UDP do not offer, such as dialogue control and peer authentication. This RFC works out how to offer the connectionless version of those OSI services over the Internet, using UDP as the transport underneath, so that OSI applications can be tried out without replacing the existing network.

sections.title: The Model: A Transport Service Provided by UDP
sections.content:
The ISO 8072 Addendum 1 standard describes the OSI connectionless transport services, and ISO 8602 describes the connectionless transport protocols. A defining characteristic of connectionless-mode transport transmission is the independent nature of each invocation of the service. The memo defines a Transport Service Access Point, or TSAP, that appears to be identical to the services and interfaces defined in ISO 8072 and its Addendum 1, but in fact implements the ISO T-UNIT-DATA protocol on top of UDP. In essence, the OSI T-UNIT-DATA service uses UDP as its connectionless network service provider.

The model places a TS-user on top of a TS-peer, with the TS-user reaching the service through the connectionless transport interface of ISO 8072/AD1 and the TS-peer reaching UDP through the UDP interface of RFC 768. The TS-peer is a process that implements the mapping of the connectionless transport protocols onto the UDP interface; the TS-user is a process that uses the services of the transport provider.

Each TS-user gains access to the provider at a TSAP, and the two TS-users can communicate with each other using the connectionless transport, provided there is pre-arranged knowledge about each other, such as protocol version, formats and options, because there is no negotiation before data transfer. All aspects of ISO 8072/AD1 are supported with one exception, the quality of service parameter, which is left for future study. The OSI standards do not specify the format of a TSAP selector, and neither does the memo, but implementors are pointed to the GOSIP 1.0 specification, where the TSAP selector consists of two octets and a value of one identifies the service interface between the OSI transport layer and session layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Each program that wants the OSI transport service reaches it at a TSAP, a named entry point. A separate piece of software, the TS-peer, sits between the two programs and turns each transport message into a datagram. The two programs must already agree on things like version and format, because nothing is negotiated before the first message is sent.

sections.title: Primitives and Parameter Mapping
sections.content:
The memo assumes that UDP offers two service primitives: send datagram, which sends a datagram to an IP address and destination port, and read datagram, which reads a datagram from UDP. Data can only be read from a receive port after the port has been created, which is a local matter. The memo reserves UDP port 102 for applications that implement the connectionless transport service over UDP, though as with RFC 1006 other port values may be used by prior agreement, for example through use of the OSI Directory.

The connectionless network service primitives required by ISO 8602 are emulated with those two UDP primitives. N-UNIT-DATA.REQUEST, in which a network service user asks for unit data to be sent, maps to send datagram. N-UNIT-DATA.INDICATION, in which a network service user is notified that unit data can be read, maps to read datagram.

The parameters map in the same straightforward way. The source address of the network service is the source IP address taken from the calling transport address, and the destination address is the destination IP address taken from the called transport address. Quality of service is ignored. The network service user data is a UD TPDU constructed from the T-UNIT-DATA primitive.

When the T-UNIT-DATA.REQUEST primitive is issued, the TS-peer constructs a UD TPDU and sends it as a single datagram to the desired IP address using UDP. When UDP indicates that a datagram has been received, a UD TPDU is read from UDP and a T-UNIT-DATA.INDICATION primitive is generated.
sections.plainLanguage: Two UDP operations do all the work: sending a datagram and reading one. Sending stands for the OSI request to transmit a message, and reading stands for the notification that a message has arrived. The addresses come from the transport addresses, and the quality of service setting is ignored.

sections.title: The UD TPDU Packet Format
sections.content:
The UD TPDU is carried in the data field of the UDP datagram. It has four parts. Octet 1 holds LI, the length of the header including parameters but excluding LI and the user data, with a maximum value of 254. Octet 2 holds UD, the type of TPDU, which is 01000000. Octets 3 to m hold the variable part, which carries the source and destination TSAP identifiers as parameters. The parameter code for the source TSAP is 11000001 and for the destination TSAP is 11000010. The parameter length is the length of the parameter, not including the parameter code and length fields, with a maximum value of 254, and the parameter value is the source or destination T-selector. The optional checksum parameter is not required in the variable part, since the checksum field in the UDP header already performs the checking.

Octets m+1 to n hold the user data, which is all of the data of the transport service data unit. The maximum network service user data allowed in the OSI connectionless network service is 64,512 octets. This limit is further constrained by the lesser maximum datagram size supported by the two communicating UDP peers, which should be known by prior agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: Each datagram carries a short header before the message. The first byte gives the header length, the second says what kind of message it is, and the bytes after that give the source and destination TSAP identifiers. The message itself follows. The UDP checksum already checks the data, so no extra checksum is added.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo has a Security Considerations section, and its entire content is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

Nothing else in the document addresses authentication, access control or confidentiality, so a reader should not take the silence as a statement that the mapping is free of security concerns. What the document does say about how the service is used is that the two TS-users need pre-arranged knowledge about each other, such as protocol version, formats and options, since there is no negotiation before data transfer, and that the port number to use may be agreed in advance, for example through the OSI Directory.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security at all. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed, so nothing here should be read as a claim that the mapping is safe.
